blocks.title: Network topology
blocks.text: Network topology is the layout of a computer network: how the devices and cables are arranged. Physical topology shows the actual connections; logical topology shows how data flows in the network.
The topology affects the network's performance and maintenance. Five common topologies are bus, star, ring, mesh and tree (Figs 1.8 to 1.12).

items: Bus: all devices are connected to a single main cable, with a terminator at each end; data travels along the cable to every device. It is simple and cheap and suits small networks, but a fault in the main cable stops the entire network, so it is not good for large networks.

blocks.alt: Bus topology: six devices (two desktop computers, a laptop, two servers and a printer) each joined by a short cable to one long main cable; each end of the main cable has a terminator, labelled Terminator.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.8: Bus Topology (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.8).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 1.8 breaks the main cable in the middle and hangs two of the six devices only on a thin line between devices. In a bus topology every device connects to one continuous main cable, as drawn above.

items: Star: all devices connect to a central hub or switch, and data passes through the central device. It is easy to manage and expand, and the failure of one device does not affect the others, but the failure of the central device stops the network. It is widely used in modern networks.

blocks.alt: Star topology: a desktop computer, a mobile phone, a laptop and a printer each joined by a dashed link, with an arrow, to one central hub or switch.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.9: Star Topology (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.9).

items: Ring: devices are connected in a circular path and data moves in one direction around the ring, each device receiving the data and passing it along. The failure of one device can affect the whole network; it is more complex than a bus and rarely used today.

blocks.alt: Ring topology: devices placed on one circular cable: two tower computers, two desktop computers, a laptop, a printer and a globe with a Wi-Fi sign at the top.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.10: Ring Topology (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.10).

items: Mesh: each device is connected to many other devices, so there are multiple paths for data. If one link fails, data uses another path, which makes the network reliable and fault-tolerant, but it is expensive and complex. It is used in large and critical networks.

blocks.alt: Mesh topology: five devices (a globe with a Wi-Fi sign, two desktop computers, a laptop and a printer), each joined by a separate line to every other device.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.11: Mesh Topology (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.11).

items: Tree: devices are arranged in a hierarchy like a tree. It combines bus and star: several star networks are connected to a central backbone, and data flows from the root (main node) to the branches and sub-branches. It is easy to expand and manage for large networks, but a backbone failure can affect the entire network. It is common in large organisations.

blocks.alt: Tree topology: a vertical Backbone Cable with end caps. Concentrator (hub) S1 joins nodes A, B and C; concentrator S2 joins nodes D, E and F; a third concentrator (hub), fed from S2, joins nodes G, H and I. A server is joined directly to the backbone. Labels: Nodes, S1, S2, Concentrator (Hub), Server, Backbone Cable.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.12: Tree Topology (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.12).

blocks.title: Class activity
blocks.text: Students stand in a circle and pass a message along; discuss what happens if one student stops.

blocks.caption: Table 1.1 Advantages and disadvantages of network topologies
rows: Simple and easy to install; needs less cable; cost-effective
Main-cable failure affects the whole network; difficult to troubleshoot; performance falls as devices are added
Easy to install and manage; one device failing does not affect others; easy to detect faults
Central-device failure stops the entire network; needs more cable; higher cost
Data flows in an organised way; no data collisions; equal access for all devices
One device failing affects the whole network; difficult to add or remove devices; rarely used today
Highly reliable and fault-tolerant; multiple paths for data; high security
Very expensive; complex installation; needs a large number of cables
Easy to expand; suitable for large networks; hierarchical management
Backbone failure affects the whole network; complex setup; more cabling needed

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Some topologies are simple and cheap; others are reliable but costly. Some are easy to expand and others are difficult to manage. The choice depends on the network's needs.
